The ideal pension system has one to three workers for each pensioner. This ensures stability. However, with more pensioners than workers, a significant problem arises; pensions will go bankrupt in 5 to 10 years. Additionally, life expectancy is increasing—old people are not dying as quickly as expected, leading to an aging crisis. This issue isn't limited to America but affects the world, particularly Japan and Germany.

In America by 2040, there will be 65 million people over 65, with 15 million being 85 or older. These individuals wield considerable power; many are in positions of authority despite their age. For instance, Joe Biden and Mitch McConnell, both retired but in their 80s, were among the most powerful men in America until they could no longer walk properly.

The aging population includes examples like Dianne Feinstein, who died in her office at 90 while serving as a senator. These people are fighting to retain power because they only give it up when they die. The US Senate, a key political institution, houses many individuals above the standard retirement age of 66, including Chuck Grassley, who is still working at 90.

Generational differences starkly contrast: young people are rebellious and want change; mature adults prefer stability; elders resist any changes, becoming reactionary when anything alters their status quo. The elderly prioritize safety over all else, making them wary of risk and uncertainty.

These factors lead to a world run by older individuals, resulting in a highly conservative system focused on preserving the status quo. This manifests as frequent lockdowns during pandemics due to old people’s fear of germs and increased police presence for social control rather than enforcement of laws. For example, in Canada, parents cannot discipline their children privately but can report them to the police, who will intervene regularly.

In essence, this shift towards an elderly-led world means a society that prioritizes safety over freedom and innovation.
